title: The Life of a Cicada
subtitle: From underground nymph to summer singer
coreQuestion: Why is this little insect from the soil hurrying up the tree?
learningGoals: Know that a cicada is an insect and its young stage is called a nymph.
Understand a cicada life cycle as egg, nymph, and adult.
Know that cicadas do not have a pupa stage like butterflies do.
Practice quiet observation without touching a molting cicada.
misconceptions: A cicada nymph is a different animal and will not become a cicada.
All insects have a pupa stage like butterflies.
A nymph climbing from soil is just wandering around.
It is okay to pick up a molting cicada for a closer look.

observationContext.scene: a summer dusk trail beside tree roots
observationContext.trigger: finding a dark cicada nymph that had just emerged from soil and was looking for a place to molt
observationContext.safetyNote: Observe quietly. Do not touch or disturb the molting process.

learningFlow.label: Real Discovery
learningFlow.childPrompt: Start with the real clue beside the tree roots: where did this little insect come from, and where is it going?

learningFlow.label: Recognize the Nymph
learningFlow.childPrompt: Notice that this is not a random little insect. It is a young cicada.

learningFlow.label: Life Cycle
learningFlow.childPrompt: Connect eggs, nymphs, shells, and adults into one growth path.

learningFlow.label: Molting Process
learningFlow.childPrompt: Trace how it moves from underground life to molting on a tree trunk.

learningFlow.label: Common Mix-ups
learningFlow.childPrompt: Compare cicadas with butterflies and dragonflies: who has a pupa, and where do young stages live?

learningFlow.label: Observation Tasks
learningFlow.childPrompt: Now try tapping and deciding for yourself: which clues matter most?

learningFlow.label: Retell and Extend
learningFlow.childPrompt: Use your own words to tell what a cicada goes through, then explore related topics.

hero.title: The Life of a Cicada
hero.lead: Start with a dark cicada nymph beside a tree root and discover why it climbs upward before becoming a summer singer.
hero.sceneExplanation: The main scene is a summer dusk trail with tree roots, soil, a small emergence hole, and a cicada nymph moving toward bark. Xiao Yutou and his younger brother observe quietly with a flashlight. Hotspots guide children to notice the nymph, the hole, the tree trunk, and the rule: observe without disturbing.
hero.childPrompt: Where did the little insect come from? Where is it going?
hero.parentPrompt: Let the child describe real clues first, then introduce cicada nymph, molting, and incomplete metamorphosis.

classificationGroups.name: It is an insect
classificationGroups.childExplanation: A cicada is an insect. A young cicada is called a nymph, and it becomes a winged adult.
classificationGroups.parentNote: For ages 4-8, focus on cicada as insect and nymph to adult.
classificationGroups.misconception: A cicada nymph is not a different animal. It is a young cicada.

classificationGroups.name: Life has stages
classificationGroups.childExplanation: A cicada starts as an egg, grows as a nymph underground, and then molts into an adult.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use egg -> nymph -> adult as the main line. Save complicated year counts for later.
classificationGroups.misconception: A cicada is not born ready to fly and does not live only in trees.

classificationGroups.name: A change without a pupa
classificationGroups.childExplanation: A cicada does not have a pupa like a butterfly. It grows as a nymph and molts into an adult.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use incomplete metamorphosis as a comparison idea, not as a term to memorize.
classificationGroups.misconception: Not every insect has a pupa stage.

representativeObjects.name: Cicada eggs in a twig
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A cicada lays eggs inside small twigs. The life cycle begins there.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking all insect eggs sit on leaves.

representativeObjects.name: Underground nymph
representativeObjects.childExplanation: The young nymph goes into soil and grows near plant roots.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking young cicadas live on tree branches.

representativeObjects.name: Emerging nymph
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A mature nymph comes out of the soil and looks for a tree trunk or another steady place.
representativeObjects.visualHint: emergence hole, strong front legs, moving to bark

representativeObjects.name: Tree trunk
representativeObjects.childExplanation: The trunk helps the nymph grip firmly while it molts.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking any place is equally good for molting.

representativeObjects.name: Cicada shell
representativeObjects.childExplanation: After molting, the old outer shell stays on the bark like a tiny empty case.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking the shell is a dead insect.

representativeObjects.name: Newly molted adult
representativeObjects.childExplanation: The new adult is soft at first. Its wings need time to open and harden.
representativeObjects.visualHint: pale body, transparent wings, hanging near shell
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking it can fly away immediately.

representativeObjects.name: Adult cicada
representativeObjects.childExplanation: The adult has wings, sings, mates, and lays eggs so the life cycle can continue.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking every singing cicada is the same individual.

representativeObjects.name: Butterfly pupa
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A butterfly has a pupa stage. A cicada does not.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking a cicada also becomes a pupa.

steps.childExplanation: Cicada eggs are placed inside a small twig.
steps.parentNote: Keep the key place: inside a twig.

steps.childExplanation: A tiny nymph hatches, falls to the ground, and goes into the soil.
steps.parentNote: This connects the tree and underground parts of the cycle.

steps.childExplanation: The nymph grows slowly underground near roots.
steps.parentNote: Mention plant sap only if the child asks.

steps.childExplanation: A mature nymph climbs out of a small hole and moves toward a tree or plant.
steps.parentNote: It is preparing to molt, not wandering.

steps.childExplanation: It grips the bark, the old shell opens, and the new adult slowly comes out.
The adult opens its wings, sings, mates, and lays eggs.
steps.parentNote: Keep adult behavior light and simple.

secondaryMechanism.title: Why does the nymph climb a tree?

steps.childExplanation: A vertical tree trunk gives the nymph a steady place to grip.
During molting, the body needs to stay steady.
steps.parentNote: No need to discuss failure risks.

steps.childExplanation: The old outer shell opens along the back, and the new body comes out slowly.
steps.parentNote: Connect this to finding empty cicada shells.

steps.childExplanation: The new adult unfolds its wings and waits for its body to harden.
steps.parentNote: Remind children not to touch a molting cicada.

comparePairs.title: Cicada vs Butterfly

b.name: Butterfly
points: caterpillar and pupa stages are obvious

comparePairs.childConclusion: A cicada has no pupa. A butterfly has a pupa.

comparePairs.title: Cicada vs Dragonfly
comparePairs.childConclusion: Both have no pupa, but their nymphs live in different places.

comparePairs.title: Nymph vs Adult
comparePairs.childConclusion: One living thing can look and act different at different stages.

clickTasks.title: Put the cicada life cycle in order
clickTasks.successCopy: Correct! A cicada starts as an egg, grows underground, then molts into a flying adult.
clickTasks.wrongHint: Think: does it live underground before or after it can fly?

clickTasks.title: Find a good molting place
clickTasks.prompt: Where should the nymph climb to molt?

wrongHints.mud: It needs a firm support, not flat mud.
wrongHints.puddle: A puddle is not a good molting place.
wrongHints.thinLeaf: A thin blade may not be steady enough.

clickTasks.successCopy: Yes! A vertical trunk helps the nymph hold still and molt.

clickTasks.title: Find the cicada shell
clickTasks.prompt: Find the empty shell on the bark.
clickTasks.successCopy: You found it! A cicada shell is the old outer case left after molting.
clickTasks.wrongHint: Look for a small empty shell attached to the bark.

clickTasks.title: Who has a pupa?
clickTasks.prompt: Which one has a pupa stage?

wrongHints.cicada: A cicada molts from nymph to adult without a pupa.
wrongHints.dragonfly: A dragonfly also has no pupa.

clickTasks.successCopy: Correct! A butterfly has a pupa, but a cicada does not.

speakTemplates: It climbs onto a ____ to molt.
A cicada is different from a butterfly because ____.
parentTips: Let the child describe what they see before naming the stage.
Connect the page to real observation: where did it come from, and why is it climbing?
If you see a molting cicada, observe quietly and do not touch it.
Use three comparison questions: where does it live, how does it change, and does it have a pupa?

visualEvidenceBindings.observePrompt: Compare visual clues for Cicada and Butterfly.
visualEvidenceBindings.evidenceCopy: Cicada: egg -> nymph -> adult; no pupa; nymph often lives underground. Butterfly: egg -> larva -> pupa -> adult; has a pupa; caterpillar and pupa stages are obvious. A cicada has no pupa. A butterfly has a pupa.

visualEvidenceBindings.observePrompt: Compare visual clues for Cicada and Dragonfly.
visualEvidenceBindings.evidenceCopy: Cicada: nymph lives underground; adult often sings in trees; no pupa. Dragonfly: nymph lives in water; adult flies in the air; also no pupa. Both have no pupa, but their nymphs live in different places.

visualEvidenceBindings.observePrompt: Compare visual clues for Cicada nymph and Adult cicada.
visualEvidenceBindings.evidenceCopy: Cicada nymph: no wings; climbs and digs; prepares to molt. Adult cicada: transparent wings; can fly; sings in summer. One living thing can look and act different at different stages.
